Introduction

Compounds of chlorine are available which have 
varying degrees of usefulness in treating water and wastewater. These compounds 
include the hypochlorite of calcium or sodium, chloramines produced by reacting 
chlorine with ammonia, chlorine dioxide, and chlorine donor complexes such as 
chlorinated cyanurates.

A number of reactions can occur when chlorine 
 is added to natural waters. Some of the most prominent chlorine applications 
 are:

1. 
 Disinfection.

2. 
 Removal of ammonia 
 and other nitrogenous organics.

3. 
 Control of taste and 
 odor.

4. 
 Hydrogen sulfide 
 oxidation.

5. 
 Iron and manganese 
 oxidation.

6. 
 Destruction of 
 organic matter.

7. 
 Color reduction.

8. 
 Control of slime and 
 algae.

9. 
 Control of iron, 
 manganese and sulfate-reducing bacteria.

Information
Principles

In chemically pure water, elemental chlorine 
reacts with the water and hydrolyzes to hypochlorous acid (HOCI) and 
hydrochloric acid (HCL):

Cl2 + H2O 
= HOCL + HCL
Chlorine + Water = Hypochlorous Acid + Hydrochloric Acid
HOCL = H+ + OCl -
Hypochlorous = hydrogen + hypochlorite

Acid 
 Ion Ion
When pH is above 3.0 and the chlorine concentration is less than 1000 ppm:

The 
 first reaction is almost instantaneous, and for all practical purposes 
 completely irreversible.

The second reaction, the dissociation of hypochlorous 
 acid to hypochlorite ions (OCl-) and hydrogen ions (H+), is reversible and the 
 equilibrium condition depends on pH and temperature. Because the dissociation 
 is so rapid, the equilibrium ratio at any given pH remains constant even 
 though the hypochlorous acid concentration may be decreasing (see figure1).

The prime oxidizing agents in water are hypochlorous acid, and to a much 
 lesser degree, hypochlorite ions. Any unreacted excess of hypochlorous acid 
 and hypochlorite ion is classified as free available residual chlorine.
Definations

The oxidation-reduction potential is a measure of the tendency of chlorine to 
 react with other materials, is not a measure of the speed with which these 
 reactions occur. As the pH increases, the chemical reactivity of chlorine 
 decreases; as temperature increases, reactions proceed more rapidly.

The oxidation reactions of chlorine with such inorganic reducing agents as 
 sulfides, sulfites and nitrites are generally very rapid. Some dissolved 
 organic materials also react rapidly with chlorine, but the completion of many 
 organic-chlorine reactions may take hours.

Chlorine demand is defined as the difference between the amount of chlorine 
 applied to a water and the amount of free combined or total available 
 chlorine which remains after a specific contact time.

Breakpoint chlorination is the addition of chlorine to water until the 
 chlorine demand has been satisfied, and further additions produce a residual 
 chlorine 
 which is directly proportional to the amount added beyond the breakpoint.

Residual chlorine is the total amount of free and combined chlorine remaining 
 in water after the chlorine demand has been satisfied. Free residual 
 chlorination is the application of chlorine to water to produce a free 
 available chlorine residual. Free available residual chlorine is the residual 
 chlorine which exists in water as hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite ions.

Combined residual chlorination is the application of chlorine to water to 
 produce with natural or added ammonia, a combined available chlorine 
 residual. Combined available residual chlorine is the chlorine residual which 
 exists in water in chemical combination with ammonia or other organic nitrogen 
 compounds (chloramines) after the waters chlorine demand has been satisfied.

Pre-chlorination is the application of chlorine to water prior to other 
 treatment processes. Re-chlorination is the application of chlorine at one or 
 more points of a system to water which has already been chlorinated. 
 Post-chlorination is the application of chlorine to a water effluent from 
 other treatment processes. De-chlorination is partially or completely reducing 
 residual chlorine by chemical or physical means.
Disinfection

Disinfecting water implies the destructive deactivation of pathogenic and 
 other organisms. This does not necessarily mean sterilization, nor the

destruction of all living organisms. Sterilization is largely confined to 
 medical and other specialized industrial applications.

The bactericidal action of chlorine is considered to be physiochemical, as a 
 result of the rapid oxidizing power of hypochlorous acid.

However the events surrounding the killing are obscure, theoretically, 
 bacterical cells are destroyed by the irreversible chemical reaction of 
 chlorine with a host of cellular components. This would explain the extreme 
 sensitivity of some organisms to chlorine, but fails to account for the 
 differences in sensitivity manifested by a variety of microbial types. It is 
 not known by what mechanism certain forms can withstand chlorine concentrations 
 well above those lethal for other forms.

Hypochlorous acid reacting with ammonia, ammonia salts or amines to form 
 chloramines will reduce the disinfecting ability of chlorine.
The formation of chloramines follows these reactions:

HOCL 
 + NH3 = NH2CL 
 + H2O

Hypochlorous 
 Acid + Ammonia = 
 Monochloramine + Water
2HOCL + NH3 = NHCL2 + 2H2O

Hypochlorous 
 Acid + Ammonia = Dichloramine 
 + Water

The pH of the treated water determines which product will be formed. At pH 
 8.5 monochloramine is the major product, at about 4.5 dichloramine is the 
 major product, between these pH value mixtures of the two prevail and below 
 pH 4.5 nitrogen trichloride is the predominant reaction product.

Where chloramines occur, a longer exposure time or an increased chlorine 
 concentration is necessary to achieve comparable bacterial reduction. The 
 oxidizing properties of chlorine are substantially lower in such combinations 
 and the reaction of chlorine with organic matter is retarded. This helps to 
 maintain a stable residual in outlying water distribution system. Although 
 this combined residual is ordinarily more stable than a free chlorine 
 residual, its lower bactericidal qualities require maintaining higher 
 residuals.
Breakpoint Chlorination

Normal chlorination of water is generally described as marginal. Very simply, 
 breakpoint chlorination is the application of enough chlorine, after the 
 chlorine demand has been satisfied, to maintain free available chlorine 
 residuals. add mg chlorine to water which contains ammonia or 
 nitrogen-containing organic matter will first produce an increased combined 
 chlorine residual.

After the maximum residual is reached, further chlorine doses will decrease 
 the residual values because the combined available chlorine residuals formed 
 when the chlorine was first added, will decompose. Decrease of the chlorine 
 residual will not being until the additional chlorine is at least eight or 
 more times the amount of free ammonia present. If this chlorine-ammonia ratio 
 is less than 8:1.for example 4:1 chloramines will form, and the breakpoint 
 reactions will not occur. When this instantaneous chlorine demand is high, the 
 chlorine requirements needed to provide free available chlorine residuals may 
 be 20 or more times the quantity of ammonia present.
Figure 2

Once the chlorine demand has been satisfied (the breakpoint is reached), free 
 chlorine appears as available residual and increases in direct proportion to 
 the chlorine applied as shown in (figure 2) a theoretical breakpoint curve. As 
 free available residual develops, it usually destroys tastes and odors, kills 
 almost all bacteria and oxidizes organic matter. However, the free residual is 
 quite unstable and is easily dissipated.

A typical breakpoint curve is more like that shown in (figure 3). The initial 
 chlorine dosage produces no residual because of an immediate chlorine demand 
 caused by fast reacting ions. Higher chlorine dosages develop chloramines 
 which are shown in the total chlorine residual. At higher chlorine dosages, 
 the slope to breakpoint, free chlorine residuals develop.

Breakpoint chlorination can also control slime and algae growths, aid 
 coagulation, oxidize iron and manganese, remove ammonia from boiler makeup 
 water and generally improve water quality in the treatment cycle or in the 
 distribution system.
Figure 3
Hypochlorination

The most common commercial forms of 
 hypochlorite include sodium hypochlorite with about 15 % available 
 chlorine, and high test calcium hypochlorite with 70% available 
 chlorine. The hypochlorite salt most widely used to treat industrial waters is 
 calcium hypochlorite,Ca(OCI)2. When this material dissolves in 
 water, ionization occurs:

Ca(OCI)2 
 = Ca-- + 2(OCI)-

Calcium 
 Hypochlorite = Calcium Ions + Hypochlorite 
 Ions

The hypochlorite ions establish an 
 equilibrium with hydrogen ions, depending on pH, as does gaseous chlorine. The 
 effect of pH is significant. Solutions of hypochlorite contain excess alkali 
 which tends to raise the pH. And in some hard waters, calcium carbonate 
 precipitates to cause scale problems. Usually, adding a complex phosphate will 
 overcome this difficulty. In other cases, the high alkalinity of the 
 hypochlorite treatment improves the quality of soft and highly corrosive 
 waters.

Although calcium hypochlorite is soluble in water, when it dissolves in hard 
 water, it often produces a precipitate. To feed calcium hypochlorite as a 
 liquid, solutions should be prepared at approximately 1-2 % 
 available chlorine.

Sodium hypochlorite, NaOCl, is available in several forms, ranging from the 
 familiar grocery store bleaches at a concentration of about 5 % , to 
 commercial laundry bleaches at a concentration of 12-15%. Most are 
 quite unstable.

Sodium hypochlorite may be fed satisfactorily in the normal 15% available chlorine strength or diluted with water. All hypochlorites are 
 somewhat harmful to skin and must be handled carefully. Satisfactory 
 corrosionresistant materials should be used for strong and dispensing 
 hypochlorites.
De-Chlorination

Activated carbon or such chemical 
 reducing agents as sulfur dioxide, sodium sulfite, sodium bisulfite or sodium 
 thiosulfate will dechlorinate water, but may also promote the growth of 
 bacteria which use the sulfur forms. Prolonged storage in open reservoirs will 
 also de-chlorinate water effectively through the action of ultraviolet 
 radiation in sunlight.

De-chlorination may be desirable for either public or industrial water 
 supplies. Reducing or removing the chlorinous taste from public water may be 
 necessary. High chlorine residuals which adversely affect many industrial 
 processes must be removed or reduced. Also, residual chlorine adversely 
 affects some resins used in ion exchange softeners and demineralizers. 
 Consequently, de-chlorination is required ahead of these units.

Other Uses and Effects of 
Chlorine

In addition to serving as bactericides, chlorine and chlorine compounds are 
 used to reduce objectionable tastes and odors from drinking water; oxidize 
 iron, manganese and hydrogen sulfide and aid in their removal, and oxidize, 
 de-color and destroy organic matter.

Chlorine, injected into sewage and industrial wastes before they are 
 discharged to the receiving stream. will reduce bacteria and destroy such 
 chemicals as sulfides, sulfites and ferrous ion which may react directly with 
 oxygen. Chlorine is widely used in once-through and recirculating cooling 
 water systems to control slime and algae.

Chlorine, a long with a coagulant, is often applied to the raw water in 
 clarification processes. Such pre-chlorination improves coagulation because of 
 the action of chlorine on the organic material in the water. It also reduces 
 tastes, odor and color-production materials by oxidizing them, reduces 
 biological loading, and oxidizes iron and manganese to facilitate removal by 
 settling and filtration.

Chlorine is a successful activating agent for sodium silicate, in the 
 preparation of the coagulant aid, activated silica. This process has the 
 advantage that the chlorine used for the activation is available for other 
 purposes.

Many process water are chlorinated to control bacteria and slime-producing 
 organisms. Direct contact of water containing a chlorine residual with food 
 products is avoided in the food industries because of possible taste effects 
 in canned or frozen foods. Before using chlorinated water in food processing, 
 de-chlorination is general practice. Also, excessive chlorine affects the 
 smoothness and brightness of materials in the plating industry.

Paper mills, which produce fine paper, usually establish very critical limits 
 for chlorine residuals.

The concentration of chlorine required to control plankton and algae in 
 reservoirs varies from 0.2 to 3.0 ppm, depending on the sensitivity and type of 
 organisms present. Concentrations as great as 50 ppm may be needed to destroy 
 some types. Free available chlorine in water is toxic to fish and other 
 aquatic life at low concentrations. Combined with cyanide phenols and other 
 substances, chlorine may be even more toxic to aquatic forms of life.

Little specific data is available to define the limits of physiological 
 tolerance for chlorine in potable water. But it is generally agreed that as 
 soon as water is swallowed, the small amounts of chlorine present are 
 destroyed by reaction with saliva and gastric juices.
Feeding Equipment

Chlorination equipment is commercially 
 available for both liquefied chlorine gas and solutions of sodium 
 hypochlorite. Calcium hypochlorite is a powder and is generally added by shot 
 feeding.

Liquid chlorine is the least expensive form of chlorine and is generally used 
 except on smaller applications. Because of the hazards of a chlorine leak, 
 feeding equipment is designed to reduce chlorine gas pressure to below 
 atmospheric as soon as possible. Such operation causes any leaks to be into 
 the feeding system rather than out to the surrounding atmosphere (see figure 
 4).

Depending on the quantity required, sodium hypochlorite feeders are either 
 metering pumps or flow-controlled rotameter indicators. Because sodium 
 hypochlorite solutions contain both chlorine and some excess caustic soda, the 
 solutions are both corrosive and highly alkaline. Although less dangerous than 
 chlorine gas, hypochlorite solutions require very carefully selected feeding 
 equipment.
